What it is

Smaart-style analysis, without the licence fee or the SPL meter.

Fractional-octave RTA

1 octave down to 1/48 oct, drawn as bars or a line, with peak hold, track peak, a Y offset and averaging set to none, fast, slow or infinite. Touch the plot and the readout follows the line exactly — 213 Hz reads 213, not the nearest band centre. Tap once for marker A, again for B, drag either line, then zoom in on just that span.

Two inputs at once

Set the input channel to 1+2 and input 1 and input 2 are analysed separately and overlaid on the RTA — a measurement mic against a console feed, so you can see what the room is doing to what the desk is sending. Each input has its own trim, and the spectrograph can follow either one.

Spectrograph

Same frequency axis as the RTA with time scrolling upward, so the two plots read together. Min and max level sliders sit on the graph itself, and dragging up or down scrolls back through the history. Length, smoothing and rewind are in Settings.

Target curves

Targets for wherever you work, overlaid on the RTA: genre house curves (speech, acoustic, pop, rock, EDM), stage monitor wedges, car cabins, home theatre, stereo listening rooms and cinema X-curves — plus your own curve imported from JSON or CSV.

Captured traces

Freeze a response, keep it on screen for comparison, name it, offset it, then delete a row with one tap (and undo it). Export the set as JSON or CSV, or send the live response out as a 31-band graphic-EQ file for the processor.

How to use it

Twenty seconds from opening the link to seeing a response.

  1. Open it and start. Tap Open RTA Daddy, then Start measurement and allow the microphone when the browser asks. No mic to hand? Demo signal runs a synthetic programme so you can try every control.
  2. Pick your input. Under Settings → Input, choose the built-in mic or a USB interface, then take the mix, a single side with L / R, or both channels separately with 1+2. Not sure what the browser actually gave you? Test input on the start screen — or Settings → Input → Input self-test — shows the channel count, sample rate and a live meter for each channel, so you can confirm both sides of an interface before measuring.
  3. Level it in one tap. Press Auto Trim in the top bar and the input trim moves so the loudest band sits just under the top of the plot — far easier to read than a curve squashed against the floor. The trim is remembered per input, so your measurement mic and the tablet's own mic each keep their own setting.
  4. Set banding and averaging. Both live in the top bar — 1/3 or 1/6 octave for tonal balance, 1/24 or 1/48 for detail.
  5. Read the plots. Spectrograph on top with frequency across the bottom and time rising; RTA underneath. Touch or drag across either plot for a frequency and level readout — the spectrograph also says how far back the row under your finger is.
  6. Capture a trace. Capture stores the current response so you can compare before and after, then export it for your notes.

Gestures worth knowing

  • Tap the RTA — set marker A, tap again for B; drag either line to move it and Zoom to fill the axis with that span
  • Pinch or scroll — zoom the frequency axis
  • Trim + / − — nudge the input trim a decibel at a time from the right-hand rail, or tap the number to put it back to 0
  • Drag up or down on the spectrograph — scroll back through the history
  • Min / Max on the spectrograph — set its level window without opening Settings
  • Drag the divider — resize the spectrograph against the RTA
  • Pause — freeze both plots without stopping the audio
  • Graph / RTA — give one plot the whole screen, tap again to split
  • Full — true fullscreen, with no browser bars
  • Fit — return the view to full range

Install it like an app

Optional, but it removes the browser chrome and gives you a home-screen icon.

Android

Open the link in Chrome, tap the ⋮ menu, then Add to Home screen or Install app. It launches full-screen, in landscape or portrait.

iPhone / iPad

Open in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. Note that iOS has no screen wake-lock API, so the tablet may dim during long sessions.

Microphone access needs a secure context. This site is served over HTTPS, which satisfies that — but opening a saved copy from a local folder will not.

Adding it to the home screen is also the easiest way to keep it offline-ready: do it once on a good connection and it will open later with no network at all — no Wi-Fi, no data, no server. The icon is only a shortcut to the copy the browser already holds, so nothing extra is downloaded.

Questions

Is it really free?

Yes. No account, no trial, no feature locks, and nothing to buy later. RTA Daddy is free for the community — made by an audio engineer, for audio engineers — and the whole analyzer is a static page that runs on your device.

What happens to my audio?

It is analysed in the browser and never uploaded or recorded. Nothing is sent anywhere, and there is no analytics on the audio path.

Why is there no SPL metering?

Deliberately left out. A trustworthy SPL reading needs a calibrated measurement microphone and a reference calibrator; an uncalibrated tablet mic would only produce a confident-looking wrong number.

Why does the level read lower than a hardware RTA?

Because the numbers are dBFS — decibels below digital full scale — not dB SPL in the room. Two things make them sit lower than a standalone analyzer. A browser cannot touch the analog gain on your interface, so you lose the preamp lift a hardware RTA has. And the app asks for the microphone with auto gain control, noise suppression and echo cancellation switched off, because all three reshape the spectrum; leaving them on is worth roughly 12 dB of level but costs you the shape of the curve. That trade is made on purpose: a truthful plot beats a taller one.

Narrow banding reads lower again. A 1/48-octave band covers far less of the spectrum than a 1/3-octave band, so it shows less total energy — both readings are correct, they are just averaging over different widths. Music and speech also fall away with frequency, so the top octaves usually sit below the bass.

Press Auto Trim in the top bar and the input trim is set so the loudest band lands about 6 dB below the top of the plot, which is where a curve is easiest to work with. It is remembered per input device. Trim moves the reading, not the signal: signal-to-noise does not improve and a small capsule cannot be made loud. Only calibration against a known SPL reference could make these numbers agree with a meter — which is why there is no SPL readout here.

Does it work offline?

Yes — online once, offline after. The first visit downloads the whole analyzer: one page, a stylesheet, one script and its icons, about half a megabyte. A small service worker — the piece the browser keeps running for the site — stores that copy and hands it back to you every time you open the address. There is no app-store download and no installer.

From then on the microphone, the analysis and every control work with the network completely off: no Wi-Fi, no mobile data, no server.

Three things still want a connection. The first load has to reach the site at least once. Updates arrive the next time you open it online. And the visit counter at the bottom of this page just stays blank offline — it is the only thing on the site that talks to a server. Clearing this browser's site data removes the stored copy, and a different browser or device keeps its own, so those have to load online once more.

What to expect in a venue: with Wi-Fi off completely, a stored copy opens straight away. On Wi-Fi that exists but has no internet behind it — a mixer or guest network, or a login page that was never completed — the browser first tries the network and only then falls back to the stored copy, so it can take a few seconds before the plots appear. It always opens; it just is not instant on that kind of network.

What do the Min and Max sliders on the spectrograph do?

They set the level window the colours map to — the same pair as Settings → Spectrograph. Raise Min to push the noise floor to black, lower Max to keep a hot signal from saturating the plot. The window always stays at least 6 dB wide, so the graph cannot be flattened by accident.

Can I see what just happened?

Yes. Drag up or down on the spectrograph, or turn the mouse wheel over it, to walk back through the history; the rewind bar under the graph shows how far back you are. Slide it to 0 to return to live, or hit Pause to hold a moment.

Can I compare a mic against the console?

Yes. With a stereo interface, set Settings → Input → Input channel to 1+2. Input 1 and input 2 are then measured as two independent analyzers: input 1 fills the RTA and input 2 is drawn over it as a line, each with its own trim, and the spectrograph can follow either. Put the measurement mic on input 1 and a console feed on input 2 to see what the room is adding to or taking from the mix.

This is two RTAs side by side, not a transfer function. There is no phase, no coherence and no mathematical subtraction of one input from the other, so the gap you see is a level difference per band — useful for chasing a room mode, not a substitute for a Smaart TF measurement.

What should I run it on?

An Android tablet in landscape is the sweet spot: a comfortable screen and a browser that hands over the microphone cleanly. Any desktop browser works too.
